chapters.title: Chapter 2: Crude Oil and the Global Economy

lessons.title: Oil Shocks and India: Inflation, the Rupee, and the Fiscal Math

children.text: An Oil Shock Is a Double Tax on India

India imports well over four-fifths of the crude oil it consumes, which makes it one of the economies most exposed to a global oil price spike anywhere in the world. But the exposure runs through more channels than most investors track. A rising oil price does not just cost more at the pump. It widens the current account deficit, weakens the rupee, feeds directly into inflation, and forces uncomfortable fiscal choices in Delhi. This lesson walks through all four, and then shows why two of them compound each other in a way that catches people off guard.

body.text: For India, an oil price shock is a double tax. It is paid once in dollars, when the global price rises, and paid again through a weaker rupee, because the same shock that pushes up the import bill also tends to weaken the currency you're paying it in.

body.caption: How an Oil Price Spike Moves Through the Indian Economy

cells: A higher oil import bill, paid in dollars, widens the gap between what India pays for imports and earns from exports
A wider CAD increases demand for dollars to pay for oil, which by itself puts depreciation pressure on the rupee
Fuel and transport costs rise directly, and higher freight costs feed indirectly into food and manufactured goods prices within a few months
Government revenue from excise duty on petrol and diesel is a meaningful, politically sensitive lever that gets pulled to cushion consumers when prices spike

children.text: Economists commonly cite rule-of-thumb sensitivities for the first two channels, useful for building intuition even though the exact figures shift with the size of India's import bill and the state of the broader economy in any given year.

stats.label: CAD Impact of a $10/Barrel Rise
stats.context: A commonly cited rule of thumb from Indian economists and RBI commentary, not a fixed formula

stats.label: CPI Impact of a $10/Barrel Rise
stats.context: Approximate, and depends on whether the government absorbs part of the increase through excise duty cuts

children.text: The Double Whammy: Price and Currency Compound Each Other

Crude oil is priced in US dollars globally. India pays for it in dollars, but the money ultimately comes from a rupee-denominated economy. This means the cost that actually lands on India is a function of two numbers moving at once: the dollar price of oil, and the rupee-dollar exchange rate.

body.caption: Because both variables can move in the same direction during a shock, a bad quarter for India's oil bill is rarely just one bad number. It's usually two, multiplying each other.

children.text: A wider CAD from a higher oil price is itself one of the things that weakens the rupee, as the table above showed. Which means a global oil shock and a rupee depreciation are not two independent risks. They are frequently the same shock, showing up twice.

body.title: Work the Double Whammy
body.prompt: Brent crude rises from $70 to $80 a barrel, and over the same period the rupee weakens from ₹83 to ₹86 per dollar. Approximately what is the combined percentage increase in India's oil import cost, measured in rupees?
body.explanation: The price rose by about 14.3% (80/70) and the rupee weakened by about 3.6% (86/83). Because these effects multiply rather than add, the combined rupee cost increase is roughly 1.143 x 1.036, minus 1, which works out to approximately 18%, noticeably more than either effect on its own.

children.text: The Fiscal Lever: Cutting Excise Duty

Excise duty on petrol and diesel is a significant, and politically visible, source of central government revenue. When global crude spikes and pump prices become a political problem, the government's fastest lever is not subsidising oil companies, the old pre-2010s approach, but cutting excise duty to directly soften the retail price increase, at a direct cost to its own revenue.

body.label: Excise Duty Cuts During the 2021-2022 Oil Spike
body.value: Two rounds of cuts, November 2021 and May 2022
body.context: As crude prices surged, the central government cut excise duty on petrol and diesel in successive rounds to cushion consumers, trading fiscal revenue for lower pump prices. Exact rupee-per-litre figures should be checked against the original Finance Ministry notifications, since duty structures are revised periodically.

body.title: How India's Fuel Pricing Regime Has Changed

columns.label: Before Deregulation (Pre-2010 Petrol, Pre-2014 Diesel)
points: Oil marketing companies compensated for under-recoveries via government oil bonds and subsidies
Fiscal cost showed up as subsidy burden and off-balance-sheet bonds

columns.label: Since June 2017 (Dynamic Daily Pricing)
points: Retail petrol and diesel prices revised daily, tracking benchmark crude and the rupee
OMC marketing margins move with the cycle instead of being fixed by the government
Government's main lever shifts from subsidy to excise duty adjustments

body.text: This is exactly why Chapter 2's earlier lesson noted that OMCs like IOC, BPCL and HPCL can actually see margins squeezed during a sharp crude spike, even though they are the companies selling the fuel. Under daily dynamic pricing, a rapid crude rally doesn't always pass through to the pump instantly, especially when there's political pressure to hold retail prices steady, and that lag temporarily compresses marketing margins.

points: An oil price shock reaches India through four channels: the current account deficit, the rupee, consumer price inflation, and government fiscal math via excise duty.

A rule of thumb: a $10 per barrel rise in average crude prices is commonly estimated to widen India's CAD by roughly 0.3 to 0.4% of GDP and add roughly 20 to 30 basis points to CPI inflation, though the exact numbers shift year to year.

Because oil is priced in dollars, a weaker rupee and a higher oil price compound each other rather than simply adding up, which is why bad oil years for India are often worse than the headline dollar price move alone would suggest.
Excise duty cuts, not oil bonds, are now the government's main fiscal lever during a price spike, a direct trade-off between consumer relief and government revenue.
